sections.h2: Ways to sell in Port Huron
sections.html:
A Port Huron homeowner has three basic options: list with an agent, sell privately, or accept an offer from a buyer who purchases houses outright. The city is the St. Clair County seat, so the county land records office sits inside city limits.

How quickly a sale closes comes down to what is left unresolved. Clear title, permits on file and an empty house move fast on any route. An unpaid tax bill, a missing permit or a lease in place slows things, and the buyer either waits for a fix or discounts the price. The sections below cover what the city and county ask for, so you can clear those items early.

Port Huron stands where Lake Huron narrows into the St. Clair River, facing Sarnia, Ontario across the water, and the Blue Water Bridge links the two cities. The 2020 census counted 28,983 residents, and the July 1, 2025 estimate is 28,273, a 2.4% decline.

The middle owner-occupied home was valued at $149,300 for 2020 to 2024, with a middle rent of $982. Owners live in 61.7% of the homes. The city has 12,734 households averaging 2.21 people, with a middle income of $50,366. Monthly owner costs sit around $1,140 with a mortgage and $562 without.

If you inherited the house, finish the title and probate steps before listing, and start them early. Recent nearby sales are the best guide to a fair price.

sections.h2: Water, flood maps and winter weather
sections.html:
With so much shoreline, flood mapping matters. The city's planning page links flood maps, and a property in a flood plain or zone may need EGLE Water Resources approval for exterior projects. Ask the Building Inspection Division whether your parcel is mapped before you list.

Winters bring 35.5 inches of snow in a typical year, spread over 22 snowy days, and the record low is minus 19 F. Buyers' inspectors look closely at roofs, gutters and heating, so have those in good shape. Water access is the main draw for buyers, since the city owns waterfront parks, public beaches and a large municipal marina system.

sections.h2: Permits that come up before a sale
sections.html:
Port Huron's Building Inspection Division sorts permits into four groups, and a buyer's inspector tends to look at the same items.

Port Huron permit categories
Permit typeWork covered
Building permitRoofs, windows, doors, siding, decks, porches, garages, basement finishes, interior and exterior alterations
Zoning permitFences, driveways, concrete patios, hot tubs, playground equipment, pools over 24 inches deep
Mechanical permitFurnaces, air conditioners, hot water tanks, fireplaces, gas piping
Electrical permitNew circuits, water heaters, sump pumps, generators, smoke detectors
No permit neededPainting, carpeting, tile, replacing kitchen cabinets in the same layout

Going without a permit can lead to safety problems, fines, even removal of the structure, and complications when you try to sell. An owner may pull permits in place of a contractor only as the registered legal owner living in the house as a primary residence. Properties in the Historic District need Historic District Commission approval for exterior work. The Building Inspection Division answers at (810) 984-9733.

The planning department runs a Rental Certification Program, and its document center posts a Foreclosed, Vacant and Abandoned Property Registration Form. If your house has been rented or sits empty, ask the Building Inspection Division what registration or certification applies to the address and whether it passes to a buyer.

Houses inside the historic area fall under Chapter 52-576 through 52-591 of the city's Historic District ordinance, which requires a work permit for alterations, significant repairs, new construction, demolition and moving.

sections.h2: St. Clair County land records office
sections.html:
You will find the register's office at 200 Grand River Avenue, Suite 103, Port Huron, reachable at (810) 989-6930. Monday through Thursday it works from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Friday from 10:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with a lunch closing from noon to 1:00 p.m. The recording counter shuts at 4:00 p.m., and anything received later is dated 8:00 a.m. on the next business day.

  • Recording charge: a flat $30.00 for each document whatever its page count, plus $3.00 after the first instrument reference.
  • Certified copy of a recorded document: $5.00.
  • Tax certificate: required before recording a warranty deed, a land contract, or any deed with a warranty covenant, under MCL 211.135. The treasurer certifies over the counter from 9:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., closed noon to 1:00 p.m.
  • Transfer tax: $1.10 for each thousand dollars of sale amount for the county and $7.50 for each thousand for the state.

Online records go back to 1984, and there is a Property Fraud Alert sign-up. Closing agents normally carry the deed in for the seller.

Before you list, pull your deed, any probate papers, permit records and the latest tax bill. Call the Building Inspection Division about flood zones, rental certification and vacant property registration, then ask your closing agent to schedule the recording early enough to beat the 4:00 p.m. counter cutoff on closing day. If an unpaid tax bill or lease is involved, settle how it will be handled in the contract so the buyer is not surprised.

sections.h2: Clearing problems before buyers see the house
sections.html:
Most delays in a Port Huron sale trace back to three things: title, taxes and occupancy. Order a title check early so any lien or probate gap shows up while you still have time to fix it. Ask the county treasurer for the current tax status, and pay what is owed or plan to settle it from the proceeds at closing. If a tenant lives in the house, decide whether they will stay through closing or leave first, and keep the lease handy for every buyer who asks.

An empty house is easier to show and to close on. Turn on the heat in cold months, keep the yard tidy, and keep the receipts for any roof, furnace or window work so the buyer's inspector sees a documented history.

sections.h2: Listing, private sale or direct buyer on the calendar
sections.html: A listing adds showings, a buyer's loan approval, an appraisal and a repair negotiation, and each of those can add days. A private sale removes the agent but leaves you to handle the contract and the paperwork. A direct purchase can close once title is clear and the recording is scheduled. Ask each buyer for a closing date, a net figure and a list of who pays for recording, the tax certificate and transfer tax, then compare the offers on those terms rather than the headline price alone.

faqs.q: How soon can a Port Huron sale close?
faqs.a: It depends on title, taxes and any tenant. At the recording end, the St. Clair County counter closes at 4:00 p.m., and a document received after that is dated 8:00 a.m. the next business day.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for work I did before selling in Port Huron?
faqs.a: Roofs, windows, doors, siding, decks, garages and basement finishes need a building permit, and furnaces, water heaters and sump pumps need trade permits. Skipping one can cause problems when you sell.

faqs.q: Where is a Port Huron deed recorded?
faqs.a: At the St. Clair County Register of Deeds, 200 Grand River Avenue, Suite 103. A warranty deed needs a county treasurer's tax certificate first.

faqs.q: What transfer tax applies in St. Clair County?
faqs.a: The county charges $1.10 per thousand dollars of sale amount and the state charges $7.50 per thousand. Your closing statement shows the exact dollar amounts for your sale.

faqs.q: Are there flood zones to check before listing in Port Huron?
faqs.a: Yes. The city links flood maps on its planning page, and a property in a flood plain may need state approval for exterior projects. Call the Building Inspection Division at (810) 984-9733 to learn whether your parcel is mapped.
